---
title: "Zeros in count data"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

More observed zeros than a Poisson model predicts do not by themselves establish a separate zero-generating process. We examine this ambiguity in Storme's ([2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11525-024-09429-8)) French liaison study and its [Zenodo release](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.12733801). One prepared row is a final-morpheme, final-consonant, and liaison-status combination. Following the released code, the response is integer truncation of 100 times summed `freqfilms2`, not a direct token tally. The Zenodo record states no separate data license, so these notes do not redistribute it.

We first audit how the released count proxy and zeros are constructed, then compare one-process and two-process explanations without treating zero excess as proof of a mechanism.

```{r}
#| label: load-storme-zero
#| echo: true
path <- "data/storme-liaison/storme-liaison-counts.csv"
if (file.exists(path)) {
  storme <- read.csv(path)
} else {
  url <- paste0("https://zenodo.org/api/records/12733801/files/",
                "study1-data.csv/content")
  source_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
  download.file(url, source_file, mode = "wb")
  stopifnot(unname(tools::md5sum(source_file)) ==
              "8a7788489b6820822cda3f338881f77e")
  raw <- read.csv(source_file, check.names = FALSE)
  storme <- aggregate(freqfilms2 ~ final_morph + FinalConsonant + Liaison,
                      raw, sum)
  storme$reconstructed_count <- as.integer(storme$freqfilms2 * 100)
  names(storme)[1:4] <- c("final_morpheme", "final_consonant", "liaison",
                          "frequency_per_million_sum")
}
stopifnot(nrow(storme) == 11195L)
storme$liaison <- factor(storme$liaison, levels = c("no", "yes"))
storme$final_consonant <- factor(storme$final_consonant)
```

The first prepared row is an actual release-derived cell:

```{r}
#| label: inspect-one-storme-cell
storme[1L, c(
  "final_morpheme", "final_consonant", "liaison",
  "frequency_per_million_sum", "reconstructed_count"
)]
```

If $f_{h}$ denotes `freqfilms2` for source row $h$ in a particular morpheme--consonant--liaison cell, the released preparation computes

$$
y
=
\operatorname{trunc}
\left(
100\sum_h f_h
\right).
$$

Thus a zero may be produced by zero summed frequency or by positive summed frequency below $.01$ before truncation. It is not an observed count of liaison tokens.

We fit additive Poisson and negative-binomial baselines with the same mean formula. The negative binomial allows

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i\mid\mu_i]=\mu_i+\frac{\mu_i^2}{\theta},
$$

so ordinary heterogeneity can increase both tails, including zero mass.

A zero-inflated count model would instead introduce a second process. With structural-zero probability $\omega_i$ and count mean $\mu_i$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=0)
=
\omega_i+(1-\omega_i)f_{\text{count}}(0\mid\mu_i),
$$

and for $y>0$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=y)
=(1-\omega_i)f_{\text{count}}(y\mid\mu_i).
$$

Both processes can thus generate an observed zero. A linguistic analysis needs a mechanism that makes some cells structurally unable to occur before it interprets $\omega_i$.

```{r}
#| label: compare-zero-probabilities
#| echo: true
poisson_fit <- glm(reconstructed_count ~ liaison + final_consonant,
                   poisson(), storme)
nb_fit <- MASS::glm.nb(reconstructed_count ~ liaison + final_consonant,
                       data = storme, control = glm.control(maxit = 100L))
storme$observed_zero <- storme$reconstructed_count == 0L
storme$poisson_zero <- dpois(0L, fitted(poisson_fit))
storme$nb_zero <- dnbinom(0L, size = nb_fit$theta, mu = fitted(nb_fit))
zeros <- aggregate(cbind(observed_zero, poisson_zero, nb_zero) ~ liaison,
                   storme, mean)
zeros
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-zero-comparison
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
zero_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(liaison = zeros$liaison, model = "Observed", value = zeros$observed_zero),
  data.frame(liaison = zeros$liaison, model = "Poisson", value = zeros$poisson_zero),
  data.frame(liaison = zeros$liaison, model = "Negative binomial", value = zeros$nb_zero)
)
zero_long$model <- factor(zero_long$model,
                          levels = c("Observed", "Poisson", "Negative binomial"))
ggplot(zero_long, aes(model, value, shape = liaison)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = .35), size = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Probability of a zero", shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

The Poisson model assigns almost no zero mass, while the negative binomial moves toward the observed proportions without a structural-zero component. We thus do not fit a zero-inflated model here. Such a model requires a linguistically motivated process that makes some morpheme cells deterministically absent, not merely a conspicuous zero bar.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why is `reconstructed_count` not a direct token tally?
2. Which two components of a zero-inflated model can produce zero?
3. Why does extra-Poisson zero mass not prove a structural-zero process?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. It is a truncated transformation of summed frequency-per-million values. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
2. The structural component and the ordinary count component can both produce zero. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
3. Unmodeled heterogeneity or a negative-binomial count process can also increase zero probability. The mixture needs an independently motivated state. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->

</details>

The [next page](negative-binomial-regression.qmd) derives that heterogeneous count model.
